Why the Normal distribution matters so much
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

blocks.x: STAT 153 · Statistical Methods · Topic 6

So far, discrete distributions (like the Binomial) counted outcomes — number of successes, number of patients. Continuous distributions instead model measurements that can take any value on a scale — a waiting time, a blood pressure reading, a survival time. Almost every biological measurement you will ever analyse as a clinician is continuous, which makes this topic one of the most clinically useful in the whole course.

4continuous distributions covered — Uniform, Exponential, Gamma, and Normal (with the Standard Normal) Z = (X−μ)/σthe standardisation formula that converts any Normal variable into the Standard Normal, N(0,1) 68 · 95 · 99.7%proportion of a Normal population within ±1, ±2, and ±3 standard deviations of the mean
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Explain what makes a random variable "continuous", and why probabilities are read as areas under a density curve rather than as heights of bars.
2Apply the continuous Uniform distribution to model events that are equally likely over an interval — such as patient arrival or waiting times — and compute its mean, variance and probabilities.
3Apply the Exponential distribution to model the time between random medical events (arrivals, failures, survival), and use its memoryless property to reason clinically.
4Apply the Gamma distribution to model the waiting time until the k-th event (e.g. the 3rd post-operative complication, the k-th seizure), using its shape (α) and scale (β) parameters.

5Apply the Normal distribution to biological measurements (blood pressure, cholesterol, birth weight), and standardise any Normal variable to a Z-score to compute clinical probabilities and reference ranges.
6Use the Normal approximation to the Binomial for large-sample clinical trial and proportion-estimation problems.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Continuous random variable A variable that can take any value within an interval (or set of intervals) — not just whole numbers. Waiting time, blood pressure, cholesterol level and birth weight are all continuous: between any two possible values, infinitely many other values are possible.

Probability density function (PDF), f(x) A function with f(x) ≥ 0 for all x, and total area under the curve equal to 1 — i.e. ∫f(x)dx over all possible x = 1. Unlike a discrete probability, f(x) itself is not a probability; probability is the area under f(x) between two limits: P(a < X < b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx.

Why P(X = x) = 0 for a single point Because probability is an area, and a single point has zero width, the probability that a continuous variable equals any one exact value is always 0. This is why, for continuous variables, P(X < x) = P(X ≤ x) — including or excluding the boundary point makes no difference to the area.

Cumulative distribution function (CDF), F(x)
F(x) = P(X ≤ x), the running total area under f(x) up to the point x. F(x) increases from 0 to 1 as x moves from the smallest to the largest possible value, and P(a < X < b) = F(b) − F(a).
Uniform→ Exponential→ Gamma→ Normal & Standard Normal
Equally likely over an interval

The simplest continuous distribution: every value between two limits a and b is exactly as likely as any other. It is the natural starting model whenever a clinical process is scheduled or randomised evenly across a window of time.
The Uniform density and CDF

Continuous Uniform distribution, X ~ Uniform(a, b) A random variable X has a continuous uniform distribution over (a, b), with a < b, if every value in that interval is equally likely: f(x) = 1 / (b − a), for a ≤ x ≤ b; f(x) = 0 elsewhere. F(x) = (x − a) / (b − a), for a ≤ x ≤ b. The density is a flat, rectangular curve — probability over any sub-interval depends only on its length, not its position within (a, b).
Where the Uniform distribution shows up in medicine

items: 1Emergency department wait times — when patients are seen roughly evenly across a scheduling window with no particular time being more likely.
2Time between symptom onset and hospital admission — modelled as uniform when patients present at an even rate across a bounded window.
3Drug absorption rates over a time interval — when absorption is treated as equally likely across a short defined interval.
4Blood glucose levels during controlled fasting — measurements taken uniformly across a fixed fasting window.

blocks.x: Illustrative example Patients arrive at a clinic uniformly over a 60-minute period. If X is the waiting time, then X ~ Uniform(0, 60) — every minute in that hour is an equally likely arrival time.
Illustrative example The time between a patient being called from the waiting room and being seen by the doctor is uniformly distributed between 5 and 20 minutes, i.e. X ~ Uniform(5, 20).
Mean, variance and MGF

If X ~ Uniform(a, b): E(X) = (a + b) / 2 — the average value, sitting exactly halfway between a and b. Var(X) = (b − a)² / 12 — the spread of values; a wider interval means more uncertainty. MX(t) = (etb − eta) / [(b − a)t], t ≠ 0 Clinically: the mean is the average wait time, and the variance quantifies how uncertain a prediction of that wait time is.
Blood test lab: arrivals from 8:00–9:00 AM

Patients arrive for blood tests at a lab from 8:00 to 9:00 AM, with arrival times uniformly distributed across that hour. Let X be the number of minutes after 8:00 AM that a patient arrives, so X ~ Uniform(0, 60). Find: (a) the mean and standard deviation of the arrival/waiting time; (b) the probability a patient arrives more than 45 minutes after 8:00 AM; (c) the probability a patient arrives between 15 and 30 minutes after 8:00 AM.

items: 1Write the density and identify a, b.f(x) = 1/60, for 0 ≤ x ≤ 60; a = 0, b = 60
2(a) Mean: E(X) = (a + b)/2.E(X) = (0 + 60)/2 = 30 minutes
3(a) Variance and SD: Var(X) = (b − a)²/12.Var(X) = (60 − 0)²/12 = 3600/12 = 300 minutes²; SD(X) = √300 ≈ 17.32 minutes
4(b) P(X > 45) = area of the density from 45 to 60.P(X > 45) = ∫₄₅⁶⁰ (1/60) dx = (60 − 45)/60 = 15/60 = 0.25
5(c) P(15 < X < 30) = area of the density from 15 to 30.P(15 < X < 30) = ∫₁₅³⁰ (1/60) dx = (30 − 15)/60 = 15/60 = 0.25

blocks.x: Answers: mean = 30 minutes, SD ≈ 17.32 minutes; P(X > 45) = 0.25 (25% chance a patient arrives in the last 15 minutes of the hour); P(15 < X < 30) = 0.25 (25% chance a patient arrives in that 15-minute window). Both probabilities equal 0.25 here simply because both windows are the same 15-minute length — the defining feature of a uniform distribution.

items: For a Uniform distribution, probability depends only on the length of the interval you're asking about, never on where that interval sits within (a, b).
A 10-minute window anywhere inside Uniform(0, 60) always has probability 10/60 ≈ 0.167 — whether it's the first 10 minutes or the last 10 minutes.
The Uniform distribution is the natural "no information beyond the bounds" model — use it when you know the range but have no reason to think any part of that range is more likely than another.

blocks.x: Modelling time between and until events

The Exponential distribution models the time until a single random event; the Gamma distribution generalises it to the time until the k-th event. Together they are the workhorse distributions of survival analysis, reliability testing and pharmacokinetics.
What the Exponential distribution models

items: 1Time between patient arrivals at emergency departments — the gap until the next arrival.
2Survival time after disease diagnosis — time until death or relapse, under a constant-hazard assumption.
3Time until equipment failure — reliability testing of ventilators, infusion pumps and other clinical devices.
4Hospital stay duration — the length of a patient's stay, modelled as time until discharge.
5Time between contractions during labour — the gap between successive events.
6Drug half-life in pharmacokinetics — time until drug concentration decays below a therapeutic threshold.

blocks.x: Key use: survival analysis and reliability testing.
The Exponential density and CDF

Exponential distribution, X ~ Exponential(θ) or Exponential(λ) X is exponential with mean θ if F(x) = 1 − e−x/θ. Writing the rate parameter λ = 1/θ, this is equivalently: F(x) = 1 − e−λx and f(x) = λe−λx, x > 0. Example: time until the next emergency admission, averaging 2 hours between admissions, gives θ = 2, λ = 0.5.
Mean, variance and MGF

If X ~ Exponential(θ), λ = 1/θ:
E(X) = θ = 1/λ (average time between events)
Var(X) = θ² = 1/λ²
M<sub>X</sub>(t) = 1/(1 + θt) = λ/(λ − t)
Medical example: average time between cardiac arrests in an ICU is 48 hours, so θ = 48 and λ ≈ 0.0208 per hour.
The memoryless property

Memoryless property If X has an Exponential distribution, then P(X > x + a | X > x) = P(X > a). In words: the process "forgets" how long it has already waited — the chance of waiting a more units is the same no matter how long you've already waited.
Drug half-life

If a drug has already been in the body for 4 hours, the probability it remains active for 2 more hours equals the probability a freshly-administered dose lasts 2 hours — the drug's remaining "life" doesn't depend on how long it's already been circulating.
Patient survival

If a patient has already survived 1 year, the probability of surviving another year equals the probability that a newly diagnosed patient survives 1 year — under the (often simplified) exponential-hazard assumption.
Equipment reliability
A ventilator that has already run for 100 hours has the same reliability for the next 50 hours as a brand-new device would have for its first 50 hours.
Survival analysis after cancer diagnosis

Survival time after a cancer diagnosis follows an Exponential distribution with mean θ = 10 months. Find: (a) the probability a patient survives more than 10 months; (b) the probability a patient survives more than 30 months; (c) the survival time x such that 95% of patients survive at least that long.

items: 1Write the density with θ = 10.f(x) = (1/10) e<sup>−x/10</sup>, x ≥ 0
2(a) P(X > 10) = e<sup>−10/10</sup>.P(X > 10) = e<sup>−1</sup> ≈ 0.3678 (36.8% survive beyond 10 months)
3(b) P(X > 30) = e<sup>−30/10</sup>.P(X > 30) = e<sup>−3</sup> ≈ 0.0498 (about 5% survive beyond 30 months)

blocks.x: Answers: P(X > 10) ≈ 0.3678, P(X > 30) ≈ 0.0498, and only about 5% of patients survive beyond approximately 30 months (x ≈ 29.96 months).
Pharmacokinetics: drug concentration decay
Drug concentration Y follows an exponential decay with moment generating function M<sub>Y</sub>(t) = 4(4 − t)<sup>−1</sup>. Find the probability the drug remains therapeutic for at least 15 minutes.

items: 1Match the MGF to the form λ/(λ − t) to identify λ.M<sub>Y</sub>(t) = 4/(4 − t) ⇒ λ = 4, so θ = 1/λ = 1/4 hour = 15 minutes
2Write the density and convert 15 minutes to hours (Y measured in hours).f(y) = 4e<sup>−4y</sup>, y ≥ 0; 15 minutes = 1/4 hour

blocks.x: Answer: there is a 36.8% chance the drug remains therapeutic for 15 minutes or more.
What the Gamma distribution models

items: 1Time until the k-th adverse event in a clinical trial.
2Total radiation exposure accumulated over a series of treatments.
3Time until complete wound healing, when healing depends on several successive sub-processes.
4Survival time with multiple complications — waiting for several complications to accumulate.
5Total medication dose accumulated over repeated administrations.
6Time until the k-th seizure in a patient with epilepsy.

blocks.x: In short: the Gamma distribution models waiting times for multiple events, where the Exponential distribution is the special case of waiting for just one (k = 1).
The Gamma function

Gamma function, Γ(a)
Γ(a) = ∫₀^∞ x<sup>a−1</sup> e<sup>−x</sup> dx, a > 0 — essential for normalising probabilities in the Gamma distribution so its density integrates to 1.

c: Integer case, n a positive integer

blocks.x: The Gamma density and its parameters

Gamma distribution, X ~ Gamma(α, β) X has a Gamma distribution with shape parameter α > 0 and scale parameter β > 0 if: f(x) = [1 / (Γ(α)βα)] xα−1 e−x/β, x ≥ 0; f(x) = 0 elsewhere. β = scale parameter (average time between events). α = shape parameter (number of events being waited for). Interpretation: the time until α events occur, with an average time β between successive events.
Mean, variance and MGF

If X ~ Gamma(α, β):
E(X) = αβ (expected total waiting time)
Var(X) = αβ² (variability of the total waiting time)
M<sub>X</sub>(t) = (1 − βt)<sup>−α</sup>, t < 1/β

Quick example — chemotherapy side effects Average time between chemotherapy side effects is 3 days (β = 3); we wait for the 4th side effect (α = 4). Expected total wait: E(X) = αβ = 4 × 3 = 12 days. Variance: Var(X) = αβ² = 4 × 9 = 36 days²; SD = √36 = 6 days.
Time until the 3rd post-operative complication

Time until the 3rd post-operative complication follows a Gamma distribution with mean 6 weeks and standard deviation √12 weeks. Find: (a) the probability the 3rd complication occurs within 8 weeks; (b) the probability it takes more than 10 weeks.

items: 1Set up the two equations from the mean and variance.E(X) = αβ = 6; Var(X) = αβ² = (√12)² = 12
2Divide Var(X) by E(X) to isolate β, then solve for α.β = αβ²/(αβ) = 12/6 = 2 weeks; α = 6/β = 6/2 = 3
3Write the density with α = 3, β = 2 (Γ(3) = 2! = 2).f(x) = [1/(Γ(3)·2³)] x² e<sup>−x/2</sup> = (1/16) x² e<sup>−x/2</sup>, x ≥ 0
4(a) Integrate the density from 0 to 8.P(X ≤ 8) = ∫₀⁸ (1/16) x² e<sup>−x/2</sup> dx ≈ 0.7619
5(b) Use the complement rule with P(X ≤ 10) ≈ 0.8753.P(X > 10) = 1 − P(X ≤ 10) ≈ 1 − 0.8753 = 0.1247

blocks.x: Answers: α = 3, β = 2 weeks; P(3rd complication within 8 weeks) ≈ 76.2%; P(takes more than 10 weeks) ≈ 12.5%.

items: The Exponential distribution is the Gamma distribution with α = 1 — waiting for a single event.
The Gamma distribution is the natural model for waiting until the k-th event (α = k), when the events occur at a roughly constant average rate (β = average gap between events).

Only the Exponential distribution has the memoryless property — the Gamma distribution (for α > 1) does not, because "how many events have already happened" matters once you're waiting for more than one.

sections.title: Why the Normal distribution matters so much

blocks.x: The bell curve of biology

The Normal distribution is the single most important distribution in medical statistics, because so many biological measurements — from blood pressure to birth weight — genuinely cluster symmetrically around a population mean.
Why the Normal distribution matters so much

items: 1Biological measurements are often normally distributed — height, weight, blood values and many physiological quantities follow a bell-shaped pattern.
2Laboratory values follow normal distributions, which is why lab reports quote a reference range built around a mean and standard deviation.
3Diagnostic test results assume normality when interpreting how "typical" or "abnormal" a result is.
4Sample means approach normality as sample size grows, by the Central Limit Theorem — even when the underlying data are not Normal.
5Statistical inference relies on normality — many of the hypothesis tests and confidence intervals used in clinical research assume an underlying Normal distribution.

blocks.x: Medical measurements that are approximately Normal
Birth weights
Birth weights of full-term infants cluster around a population mean with a fairly symmetric spread.
Blood pressure
Systolic and diastolic blood pressure readings across a healthy population form a classic bell curve.
Cholesterol levels
Total cholesterol levels are approximately Normal, which underlies the "high cholesterol" cut-offs used clinically.
White blood cell counts
WBC counts in healthy individuals vary around a mean, and lab reference ranges are built from this distribution.
The Normal density function

Normal distribution, X ~ N(μ, σ²) X has a Normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ² if: f(x) = [1 / (σ√(2π))] e−(x−μ)²/(2σ²), −∞ < x < ∞ μ: the population mean — the "healthy reference" centre of the distribution. σ: the population standard deviation — a measure of biological variability around that centre. Example: adult systolic blood pressure, X ~ N(120, 15²) mmHg.
Mean, variance and MGF

If X ~ N(μ, σ²): E(X) = μ (population mean) Var(X) = σ² (biological variability) MX(t) = etμ + (1/2)t²σ² In practice, probabilities are computed by converting X to a Z-score and using standard Normal tables (covered in the next tab).
The empirical (68–95–99.7) rule and clinical interpretation

c: Almost always within this band if healthy

blocks.x:
Example — fasting blood glucose
If fasting glucose follows N(90, 15²) mg/dL:
90 ± 15 (75–105 mg/dL): about 68% of healthy people.
90 ± 30 (60–120 mg/dL): about 95% of healthy people.
A value outside 60–120 mg/dL may indicate an abnormality worth investigating.

blocks.title: Why does the Normal distribution matter beyond description?

items: Reference ranges quoted on lab reports (e.g. "70–130 units") are almost always built from a Normal model of healthy measurements — usually the μ ± 2σ band, covering about 95% of healthy people.

Because of the Central Limit Theorem, even measurements that are not individually Normal often produce Normally-distributed sample means once you average across enough patients — this is why so much of inferential statistics leans on the Normal distribution.

The next tab shows how any Normal variable, regardless of its own μ and σ, can be converted into the single universal Standard Normal distribution, N(0, 1), so that one set of tables can answer every clinical probability question.

blocks.x: One universal reference curve

Every Normal distribution, no matter its mean or spread, can be converted into one universal curve — the Standard Normal — by standardising. This single trick unlocks reference ranges, diagnostic-test probabilities, and even a fast approximation to the Binomial distribution.
Standardisation and the Z-score

Standard Normal distribution, Z ~ N(0, 1) The Standard Normal is the special case of the Normal distribution with mean μ = 0 and standard deviation σ = 1. Any Normal variable X ~ N(μ, σ²) can be converted to a Standard Normal Z-score by: Z = (X − μ) / σ where X = the patient's measurement, μ = the population mean, σ = the population standard deviation, and Z = the number of standard deviations X lies from the mean.

Why standardisation matters All Normal distributions are convertible to the Standard Normal — so a single set of tables (giving Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z)) can answer probability questions for any Normal-distributed measurement. Medical reference tables and most statistical tests rely on this fact.
Working with the standard Normal CDF, Φ(z)

Probability rules Φ(−k) = 1 − Φ(k) (symmetry of the curve about 0) P(Z > k) = 1 − Φ(k) P(−k ≤ Z ≤ k) = 2Φ(k) − 1 Clinically: the Z-score is the number of standard deviations a measurement lies from the mean; a larger |Z| means a more "abnormal" measurement, and results are typically compared against clinical thresholds such as 5%, 1% or 0.1%.
Benchmarks every clinician should know by heart
Step-by-step approach to a medical probability question

items: 1Identify the measurement and its parameters — the patient's value x, and the population mean μ and standard deviation σ.
2Convert to a Z-score — z = (x − μ)/σ.
3Look up the standard Normal table for Φ(z).
4Interpret clinically — Φ(z) is the proportion of the population ≤ x; 1 − Φ(z) is the proportion > x; compare the result against clinical thresholds (e.g. 5%, 1%, 0.1%).

blocks.x: Four clinical Z-score problems
Example 1 — Diagnostic test. A diagnostic test result follows Z ~ N(0, 1) in healthy people. A patient's result is 1.5. What proportion of healthy people would have a result ≥ 1.5?

items: 1Result is already a Z-score, so use the complement rule directly.P(Z ≥ 1.5) = 1 − Φ(1.5) = 1 − 0.9332

blocks.x: Answer: P(Z ≥ 1.5) = 0.0668 — only 6.7% of healthy people have a result this high or higher, making it a borderline abnormal finding.
Example 2 — Blood pressure. Systolic BP follows N(120, 20²) mmHg. What percentage of people have systolic BP between 100 and 140 mmHg?

items: 1Standardise both boundaries.z₁ = (100 − 120)/20 = −1; z₂ = (140 − 120)/20 = 1
2Apply the symmetric-interval rule.P(−1 < Z < 1) = Φ(1) − Φ(−1) = 0.6826

blocks.x: Answer: 68.3% of people have systolic BP between 100 and 140 mmHg — this is simply the μ ± 1σ range for this distribution.
Example 3 — Growth chart. A child's height is 110 cm. The population mean height is 120 cm, SD = 8 cm. Find the Z-score and the percentage of children shorter than this child.
Answer: z = −1.25; about 10.6% of children are shorter than this child — not concerning on its own, but worth monitoring over time.

Example 4 — Laboratory reference range. A lab test's reference range is 70–130 units, based on ±2 SD from a mean of 100. Find: (a) σ; (b) the percentage of results falling outside the reference range; (c) the value exceeded by only 1% of results (given z₀.₀₁ = 2.326).

items: 1(a) The range spans ±2σ, so set 2σ equal to the half-width of the range.2σ = 130 − 100 = 30 ⇒ σ = 15 units
2(b) A ±2 SD range covers 95% of a Normal population, by the empirical rule.5% fall outside the range (2.5% below 70, 2.5% above 130)
3(c) Use k = μ + σ·z₀.₀₁ to find the value exceeded by only 1%.k = 100 + 15 × 2.326 = 100 + 34.89 = 134.89

blocks.x: Answers: σ = 15 units; 5% of results fall outside 70–130; only 1% of results exceed 134.89 units.

Example 5 — Cholesterol. A patient's cholesterol is 240 mg/dL, drawn from a population with μ = 200, σ = 40 mg/dL. What percentage of the population has cholesterol ≤ 240, and what percentage has cholesterol > 240?

items: 2Look up Φ(1.0) and its complement.Φ(1.0) = 0.8413 ⇒ 1 − 0.8413 = 0.1587

blocks.x: Answer: 84.1% of the population has cholesterol ≤ 240 mg/dL, and 15.9% has cholesterol above 240 mg/dL.

Example 6 — Birth weights. Birth weights follow N(3400, 500²) grams. Find: (a) the probability a baby weighs between 3000 and 4000 grams; (b) the percentage with low birth weight (< 2500 g); (c) the weight exceeded by only 10% of babies (z₀.₉₀ = 1.282).

items: 4(c) Solve for the weight w using z₀.₉₀ = 1.282.(w − 3400)/500 = 1.282 ⇒ w = 3400 + 641 = 4041 grams

blocks.x: Answers: 67.3% weigh between 3000–4000 g; 3.6% have low birth weight (< 2500 g); only 10% of babies weigh more than 4041 grams.
Turning Z-scores into clinical judgement
Within ±2 SD
Falls in the 95% range — generally interpreted as "normal."
Between 2–3 SD
Borderline — worth monitoring over time.
Beyond ±3 SD
Likely abnormal — warrants investigation.
Normal approximation to the Binomial

When to use it The Normal approximation to the Binomial works well when the sample size is large (n ≥ 30 as a rough guide) and the success probability p is not extreme (not near 0 or 1). It is heavily used in clinical trials, proportion estimation, and study design.

Approximation formula
If X ~ Binomial(n, p), then approximately:
X ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)), where q = 1 − p.
The mean of the approximating Normal is np, and its variance is np(1 − p) — matching the Binomial's own mean and variance exactly, while letting you use Z-scores and standard Normal tables instead of Binomial sums.
Vaccine efficacy study
In a vaccine trial with 1000 participants, 85% are expected to be protected. Find the probability that between 830 and 870 participants are protected.

items: 1Set up the Binomial and its Normal approximation.X ~ Binomial(1000, 0.85) ≈ N(np, np(1−p)) = N(850, 1000×0.85×0.15) = N(850, 127.5)
2Take the square root of the variance to get the SD.SD = √127.5 ≈ 11.29
4Apply the symmetric-interval rule.P(−1.77 ≤ Z ≤ 1.77) = 2Φ(1.77) − 1 ≈ 0.9232

blocks.x: Answer: about a 92.3% chance that between 830 and 870 of the 1000 participants (83–87%) end up protected.

blocks.title: Putting it all together: reference ranges, Z-scores and clinical decisions

items: Reference ranges distinguish normal from abnormal values, almost always built as a μ ± 2σ band.
Diagnostic testing interprets how far a patient's result sits from the healthy population mean, via its Z-score.
Growth monitoring (percentile charts) is really Z-scores computed against age-specific reference populations.
Clinical trials use the Normal approximation to the Binomial for statistical analysis of proportions in large samples.
Epidemiology relies on Normal-based models for disease measurement distributions across populations.
